Name: ext4
SDKs & notable repos: tune2fs, dumpe2fs, debugfs, e2fsck — the userland toolbox every rescue story uses
Downloadable / offline docs: Kernel docs build from source (`make htmldocs`); ext4(5) man page
Notes: The default Linux filesystem. Read the journal and delayed-allocation docs once — most slow-disk interview questions end here.

Name: XFS
SDKs & notable repos: xfs_admin, xfs_repair, xfs_bmap, xfs_io — xfs_io alone teaches you the syscall surface
Notes: The scale-out workhorse: huge files and filesystems with rock-solid repair tooling. Default on RHEL for a reason.

Name: Btrfs
SDKs & notable repos: btrfs-progs; kernel tree under fs/btrfs
Downloadable / offline docs: Sphinx docs + btrfs(8) and btrfs-send(8) man pages
Notes: Copy-on-write with checksums, snapshots and send/receive in the mainline kernel. RAID5/6 reputation is historical but still interview-bait.

Name: F2FS
SDKs & notable repos: f2fs-tools (mkfs.f2fs)
Notes: Samsung's flash-friendly filesystem: log-structured where it helps, aware of FTL behaviour. The answer to designing for SSD/eMMC.

Name: bcachefs
SDKs & notable repos: bcachefs-tools — format — mount — multi-device management
Downloadable / offline docs: Online docs; man pages with the tools
Notes: Copy-on-write with full journaling, erasure coding and caching, descended from bcache. Young and still churning.

Name: overlayfs
SDKs & notable repos: upperdir/lowerdir/merged — the mechanism under every container image layer
Notes: Read the redirect model (upper vs lower and copy-up) and container image layers stop being mysterious.

Name: tmpfs
SDKs & notable repos: RAM-backed and swap-backed; /dev/shm; size= mount option
Notes: Files count against memory and swap — not disk. The classic why-did-my-container-OOM-on-/tmp question.

Name: squashfs
SDKs & notable repos: mksquashfs and unsquashfs — inside Live ISOs — container base images — embedded firmware
Downloadable / offline docs: Compress a whole root filesystem into one read-only image
Notes: Read-only and highly compressed. Pair with overlayfs when you need writability on top.

Name: exFAT
SDKs & notable repos: The interop filesystem for SD cards and USB drives
Notes: No journal, no POSIX permissions, no extended attributes. Know why you are using it — spec in category 8.

Name: NFS
SDKs & notable repos: nfs-utils — mountd — exportfs — showmount
Downloadable / offline docs: HOWTO + exports(5) and nfs(5) man pages
Notes: The network filesystem you will actually be asked about. v3 stateless vs v4 stateful is a standing interview question.

Name: OpenZFS documentation
SDKs & notable repos: zfs/zpool/zed CLIs; zfs(8) and zpool(8) man pages
Downloadable / offline docs: Full docs site plus man pages ship with distribution packages
Notes: The vocabulary factory: CoW, checksums, snapshots, send/recv, RAID-Z, ARC/L2ARC/ZIL/SLOG.

Name: OpenZFS source
SDKs & notable repos: One codebase on two platforms: Linux and FreeBSD; module + userland split
Notes: CDDL-licensed — which is why it never merged into mainline Linux. See the honest notes.

Name: ZFSBootMenu
SDKs & notable repos: Boot environments as a system-rollback mechanism
Notes: Snapshots you can boot — the clearest demonstration of what boot environments buy you.

Name: ZFS on FreeBSD
SDKs & notable repos: The ZFS chapter of the FreeBSD Handbook
Notes: FreeBSD ships OpenZFS in the base system; the Handbook's ZFS chapter is the clearest operator guide anywhere.

Name: Ceph
SDKs & notable repos: RADOS, RBD, CephFS, RGW; librados/librbd bindings in C++, Python, Go
Downloadable / offline docs: Versioned docs per release; ceph CLI help is a doc set of its own
Notes: The unified storage platform: block, object and POSIX file over one RADOS cluster. Pin docs to /en/latest — version-scoped URLs rot.

Name: Ceph source
SDKs & notable repos: CRUSH placement and BlueStore object store — the two reading targets
Notes: CRUSH is the interview topic: consistent hashing's smarter crush-map-aware cousin.

Name: GlusterFS
SDKs & notable repos: Translator architecture; brick/volume model; FUSE-mounted
Notes: Userspace distributed filesystem with humbler and more legible ambitions than Ceph.

Name: Lustre
SDKs & notable repos: MGS/MDS/MDT/OSS/OST vocabulary — the HPC workhorse behind most Top500 scratch filesystems
Notes: Where exascale computing keeps its bytes. Read for the metadata-server vs object-storage-target split.

Name: BeeGFS
SDKs & notable repos: Metadata targets + storage targets; container-based quickstart
Notes: Parallel filesystem with a transparent, well-documented architecture — the easiest parallel FS to stand up in a lab.

Name: SeaweedFS
SDKs & notable repos: Filer, FUSE mount, S3 gateway, volume servers; inspired by Facebook's Haystack paper
Notes: O(1) disk reads for billions of small files — the Haystack idea implemented and running.

Name: JuiceFS
SDKs & notable repos: Metadata engine (Redis/TiKV/SQL) + object storage = POSIX filesystem; CSI driver for Kubernetes
Notes: The cloud-native equation in one product: metadata service plus dumb object store equals a real filesystem.

Name: Garage
SDKs & notable repos: S3-compatible — geo-distributed — self-hostable — Rust
Notes: Small-scale multi-site S3 with an unusually honest design doc about quorum and consistency trade-offs.

Name: HDFS
SDKs & notable repos: NameNode/DataNode — 128 MB blocks — replication — rack awareness — WebHDFS REST
Notes: The granddaddy. The HDFS Architecture page is still the best introduction to block-replicated distributed filesystems.

Name: MinIO
SDKs & notable repos: mc client (github.com/minio/mc); S3-compatible API in a single Go binary
Notes: The fastest way to develop against an S3 dialect without a cloud account.

Name: Ceph RADOS Gateway (RGW)
SDKs & notable repos: S3- and Swift-compatible gateways backed by RADOS
Notes: When your Ceph cluster needs to speak S3. Read next to the MinIO docs to compare gateway designs.

Name: SeaweedFS S3 gateway
SDKs & notable repos: S3-compatible gateway on the filer; buckets over volume servers
Notes: Cross-reference — the main entry is in category 3. Read alongside B2 and MinIO to compare S3 dialects.

Name: Backblaze B2
SDKs & notable repos: B2_Command_Line_Tool (github.com/Backblaze/B2_Command_Line_Tool); S3-compatible endpoint
Notes: Cheap cloud object storage with a real spec. Their Drive Stats reports are the best public disk-failure data.

Name: rclone
SDKs & notable repos: 40+ backends; rclone serve s3/webdav; rsync semantics for the cloud
Notes: The universal object-storage adapter. Its per-provider pages document exactly how each S3 dialect differs.

Name: Amazon S3
SDKs & notable repos: aws-cli, boto3, aws-sdk-* — the API everyone else copies
Downloadable / offline docs: AWS docs support per-section offline/PDF export
Notes: The de facto standard. Versioning, lifecycle rules, storage classes and consistency semantics are the interview canon.

Name: LVM2
SDKs & notable repos: pvcreate/vgcreate/lvcreate; snapshots, thin provisioning, stripes, mirrors
Notes: The volume layer every sysadmin interview assumes. Do one pv→vg→lv walkthrough by hand.

Name: device-mapper
SDKs & notable repos: dm-linear, dm-mirror, dm-thin, dm-verity, dm-crypt — the table-driven block layer
Notes: The framework LVM, cryptsetup and verity are built on. dmsetup table on a running system shows it.

Name: dm-crypt / cryptsetup
SDKs & notable repos: LUKS2 header format, token plugins, cryptsetup-reencrypt
Notes: Disk encryption is a block-layer problem — not a filesystem problem — and this project is the proof.

Name: md (multiple device) RAID
SDKs & notable repos: mdadm is the userspace interface (next entry); /proc/mdstat is the state view
Notes: Software RAID 0/1/5/6/10 with online reshape. Know the difference between md RAID and LVM mirroring.

Name: mdadm
Documentation: mdadm(8) man page — authoritative and complete
SDKs & notable repos: --detail --scan --monitor; ARRAY lines in mdadm.conf
Notes: mdadm is the interface to md. Learn the three states — clean and degraded and rebuilding — and what each means for your data.

Name: NVMe specifications
SDKs & notable repos: Base 2.x spec — NVMe-oF — ZNS (zoned namespaces): the three names to know
Downloadable / offline docs: Spec PDFs downloadable free after registration
Notes: Read the admin-vs-I/O command set split and the queue-pair model. NVMe-oF extends the same command set over a network.

Name: nvme-cli
SDKs & notable repos: libnvme (github.com/linux-nvme/libnvme); nvme list — smart-log — format
Notes: The hands-on tool for every NVMe admin question. nvme smart-log is the NVMe answer to smartctl.

Name: SPDK
SDKs & notable repos: Userspace NVMe driver, event framework, pollers, bdev layer
Notes: Kernel-bypass storage: where the put-the-stack-in-userspace school lives — with the latency numbers to argue for it.

Name: Linux SCSI target (LIO / targetcli)
SDKs & notable repos: targetcli shell; iSCSI — FC — vSCSI fabric modules on LIO
Notes: How Linux exports block devices over iSCSI. Creating one LUN with targetcli makes the LUN question trivial. Initiator: open-iscsi; target lives in kernel drivers/target.

Name: virtio (virtio-blk)
SDKs & notable repos: Virtqueues; split/packed ring layouts; how every VM talks to its disks
Notes: Read the virtqueue description once and virtual machine I/O stops being magic.

Name: BorgBackup
SDKs & notable repos: Dedup — compression — authenticated encryption; SSH as the transport
Notes: What you reach for on a single box. Its docs explain dedup better than most papers.

Name: Restic
SDKs & notable repos: Native cloud backends (S3, B2, Azure, GCS), snapshots, dedup, encryption
Notes: Designed for cloud backends from day one. The design document explains the repo format.

Name: Kopia
SDKs & notable repos: Client-side encryption, policies, KopiaUI desktop app
Notes: Restic's closest cousin with a stronger policy model. Compare the two repo formats.

Name: rsync
SDKs & notable repos: Delta-transfer algorithm; rsync(1) and rsyncd.conf(5)
Notes: Not a backup system by itself — no history, no verification — but the delta algorithm is a canonical interview topic.

Name: ZFS send/recv
SDKs & notable repos: Incremental streams (zfs send -i) — raw sends of encrypted datasets — resume tokens
Notes: Replication by streaming block trees, not files. The model WAL-shipping discussions are secretly compared against.

Name: Btrfs send/receive
SDKs & notable repos: btrfs-send(8) and btrfs-receive(8); incremental streams from snapshots
Notes: The same idea as ZFS send/recv — mainline in Linux. Snapshots + send is the Linux-native replication story.

Name: Velero
SDKs & notable repos: Kubernetes cluster-state backup; plugins for cloud volume snapshots; restic/kopia integration for PVs
Notes: Cluster state plus persistent volumes — the standard answer to how-do-you-back-up-Kubernetes.

Name: fio
SDKs & notable repos: Job files; engines: libaio, io_uring, psync, rbd, http; see examples/
Notes: THE storage benchmark. Every performance interview reduces to describing the workload in a fio job.

Name: blktrace / blkparse
SDKs & notable repos: blkparse and btt — see I/O the way the block layer sees it
Notes: iostat tells you averages; blktrace shows the actual request stream with timestamps.

Name: sysstat (iostat and sar)
SDKs & notable repos: iostat -x 1 is the first command on any slow box; sar for history
Notes: %util is a trap on fast devices — see honest notes. await and queue depth carry the real signal.

Name: smartmontools
SDKs & notable repos: smartctl — SMART attributes — self-tests — error logs; NVMe health via nvme-cli
Notes: The low-level disk health tool. Companion: hdparm (name-only) — the other veteran for drive parameters and timings.

Name: ioping
SDKs & notable repos: ping for storage — latency distribution in one command
Notes: The fastest way to feel the difference between NVMe, SATA and network block storage.

Name: IO500
SDKs & notable repos: The HPC storage benchmark; full result lists published with configurations
Notes: Shows what fast-filesystem means at scale: metadata operations and IOPS — not just bandwidth.

Name: filebench
SDKs & notable repos: Workload models (fileserver, varmail, oltp) in its own workload language
Notes: Older than fio but still the standard way to model whole application I/O patterns.

Name: SQLite file format
Source / GitHub: — (the database engine itself lives in the Database Systems index)
SDKs & notable repos: B-tree pages, WAL frames, freelist, schema layer — documented byte by byte
Downloadable / offline docs: The spec is a single complete HTML page
Notes: This entry is the on-disk format; the DBMS index covers the database itself. One of very few file formats with a complete readable spec.

Name: GNU tar
SDKs & notable repos: POSIX ustar/pax vs GNU extensions; --one-file-system and --listed-incremental
Notes: The format that outlived tapes. Incremental backup semantics, block size and device independence are all in here.

Name: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)
SDKs & notable repos: Where /etc and /var and /usr and /srv must be — and why
Notes: Distributions deviate from it; interviews do not. One afternoon to read — permanent vocabulary gain.

Name: exFAT specification
SDKs & notable repos: The published spec that made the Linux exFAT implementation possible
Notes: Spec-versus-field drift in action: SD cards in the wild disagree with Microsoft's own document in instructive ways.

Name: JEDEC standards (eMMC / UFS)
SDKs & notable repos: eMMC (JESD84) and UFS (JESD220) — the embedded flash standards inside every phone and most IoT boards
Downloadable / offline docs: Standards purchasable; some documents free after registration
Notes: Paywalled. You rarely need more than knowing which standard applies and the layering (device, partition, boot areas).

Name: UEFI specifications (GPT)
SDKs & notable repos: The UEFI spec defines the GPT partition table; ACPI and Secure Boot documents also live here
Notes: Read only the partition-table section: protective MBR, GPT header, entry array, backup copy. That layout is interview-canonical.

Name: PMDK
SDKs & notable repos: libpmem — libpmemobj — pmempool — pmreorder
Notes: The programming model that made byte-addressable storage concrete: flushes — fences — transactions at memory speed.

Name: libpmemobj
SDKs & notable repos: Transactional object store — persistent pointers — layout-aware allocator
Notes: The hardware it targeted (Optane) was discontinued, but the crash-consistency ideas are permanent — the cleanest education in memory-speed persistence.

Name: DAX
SDKs & notable repos: Direct access: mmap bypasses the page cache entirely
Notes: CXL and the new-interconnect story are owned by the Computer Architecture index — this page keeps only the filesystem-side DAX note.

Name: NVDIMM admin guide
SDKs & notable repos: pmem namespaces — labels — modes; ndctl companion below
Notes: Region vs namespace and why pmem and blk modes existed. The kernel-side counterpart to the PMDK view.

Name: ndctl
SDKs & notable repos: Namespace management — region/label model — daxctl for device-DAX
Notes: libnvdimm's userland. Even with Optane gone the tooling remains the reference for how the kernel models persistent regions.
